newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Montenegro parliament speaker urges privatisation.
newsitem.headline: Montenegro parliament speaker urges privatisation.

text.p: Montenegro's parliamentary speaker called on Wednesday for more democracy, privatisation and a quick return to international financial institutions, to help Yugoslavia win foreign financial support.

"Democracy is the first request. But we must also show decisive commitment to privatisation in the whole country, because Yugoslavia is one country...It is important that the process gains intensity and quality in Serbia as well," Svetozar Marovic told reporters.
"It is ideologically absolutely wrong, unacceptable, even tragic to defend concepts of anachronistic forms of ownership," he said at a presentation of the Montenegrin tourism industry.
The junior partner in the Yugoslav federation is home to some 650,000 people and heavily reliant on tourism, iron and aluminium industries.

It refused to wait for Serbia to begin radical economic reforms and launched its own privatisation model, including voucher privatisation which has been persistently rejected by Belgrade. But the tiny republic has been hit hard by political instability in Serbia.

Three months of mass opposition protests over local election fraud affected many Montenegrin business deals with foreigners and brought privatisation to a standstill as investors waited for the situation to stabilise.

"Investors want a secure and stable country...Many contracts with foreign partners have been frozen. Without political credibility, without return to international political and financial institutions, it is unrealistic to expect any substantial foreign support.
"And without such support, privatisation has come to a halt and we must tackle the problem urgently," Marovic said.
He said it was vital for Yugoslavia to urgently address problems still barring it from world financial institutions.
"We must look at those problems, and if the problem is Kosovo then we must see how to deal with Kosovo. We frequently push problems away. But we must try to find solutions."
Serbia's impoverished southern province of Kosovo, where ethnic Albanians outnumber Serbs nine to one, is widely seen as a powder keg that could destroy peace efforts in the Balkans.
Everything that keeps Yugoslavia away from international financial institutions and the so-called outer ring of sanctions must be eliminated, Marovic added.
"It is an even more unpleasant, icier, wall of sanctions, because there was a feeling that everything was over and there were no longer barriers," he said.

The conditions for lifting the last remaining sanctions on Yugoslavia include democratisation, improvement of human rights in Kosovo, cooperation with The Hague war crimes tribunal and progress in talks on succession with other former republics.
In a country where two different economic systems co-existed, Marovic stressed the need for convergence.

"Montenegro is smaller and solved some problems faster. But It is inevitable that the same is done in Serbia. Yugoslavia cannot have any other model of developing its economy than the one known by the modern world. "There is always an alternative, but a negative one," Marovic told Reuters.
He insisted the new system would have to be based on private ownership. "That is the only condition for foreign capital to come, the only condition leading us back to the international community."
While waiting for the Yugoslav government to settle the issue with the IMF, Montenegro launched an off-shore zone project in an attempt to open up to outside investors.

"The process has begun and was halted because of political instability, but it will resume. There are talks on opening up several factories with Italian investors. There are businessmen from America and Panama looking at Montenegro," Marovic said.

"This idea can bring benefits not only to Montenegro but to Yugoslavia as a whole and it should be good to support the idea, not to trip it up." -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
